nameStory: The genus name Corambe comes from a Greek word meaning 'ornament' or 'decoration,' referring to the delicate, jewel-like appearance of these tiny sea slugs. The species name 'obscura' means 'dark' or 'hidden' in Latin, which perfectly describes this elusive little creature that's easily overlooked due to its small size and cryptic coloring.
description: Corambe obscura is a tiny nudibranch, or sea slug, that belongs to a specialized group of marine mollusks without shells. This minuscule creature typically measures less than 5 millimeters long - smaller than your pinky nail! It has a translucent to whitish body with a flattened, oval shape and lacks the colorful projections (called cerata) that many other nudibranchs display. Instead, it has a relatively smooth body with simple, club-shaped rhinophores (sensory tentacles) at the front.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small, typically 2-5mm long - about the size of a rice grain or smaller, making it easy to miss entirely

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Flattened and oval-shaped with smooth edges, lacking the frilly projections of most other sea slugs

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Translucent white to pale gray body that appears almost ghostly against dark surfaces

idTips.label: Rhinophores
idTips.description: Two simple, club-shaped sensory tentacles at the head end that are not retractable

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides very slowly across surfaces with a distinctive smooth, flowing motion

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, typically on hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or dock pilings in the lower intertidal zone. This species prefers areas with good water circulation and is often discovered during very low tides when normally submerged surfaces are briefly exposed.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm, though still requires very careful searching during extreme low tides to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation time when warmer waters make them slightly more active and visible to dedicated searchers.
seasonality.fall: Still present but becoming less active as temperatures cool, making them even more challenging to locate.
seasonality.winter: Present but largely inactive and nearly impossible to find due to reduced activity and harsh conditions.

funFact: Despite being one of the smallest marine animals you might encounter, Corambe obscura is actually a specialized predator that feeds exclusively on tiny bryozoans (moss animals) - essentially, it's a microscopic sea monster hunting even tinier colonial creatures!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be mistaken for a tiny piece of debris, a water droplet, or a small flatworm. The key difference is the smooth gliding movement and the presence of two small rhinophores at the front - flatworms typically move differently and lack these sensory structures.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the most overlooked groups of marine life in New England waters - many beachgoers walk past hundreds of tiny nudibranchs without ever noticing them, yet they play important roles in marine ecosystems as both predators and prey.
compareHints: **Note: Information about close relatives is limited due to sparse data.** Corambe obscura differs from other small nudibranchs in New England waters by its extremely simple body plan - lacking the colorful cerata, dramatic gills, or ornate projections that characterize most other sea slug families. Its closest relatives in the Corambidae family are equally tiny and simple-bodied, but Corambe obscura can be distinguished by its particularly translucent appearance and preference for bryozoan prey.
